newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-GOSDEN LANDS DERBY IN FATHER'S MEMORY.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-GOSDEN LANDS DERBY IN FATHER'S MEMORY.

text.p: John Gosden saw his dying father just lose out on the chance to train an Epsom Derby winner. Three decades later, he finally set the record straight on Saturday.
"This one is for my father," Gosden said with feeling after Benny The Dip just held on by a fast-shrinking short head to land the world's most famous horse race from Silver Patriarch.
Patience finally paid off for the Gosden dynasty that had suffered such agonising near misses on English racing's most spectacular stage.
Towser Gosden trained Charlottown with consummate skill as a two-year-old but was forced by ill health to hand over to Gordon Smyth when racing fame beckoned for the colt.
It was a bitter-sweet moment for Towser Gosden in the unsaddling enclosure at Epsom in 1966 when he got to savour Charlottown's greatest victory shortly before he died.
John Gosden, recalling the moment that is forever etched on his memory, said: "He stood in the winner's enclosure and I can see him now.
"It probably was a very fulfilling moment with a very devoid feeling for him so I'd only say to my old man somewhere up there that we finally got it right."
Apart from his father's heartache, John Gosden has savoured another trainer's triumphs and seen victory cruelly snatched from his own grasp.
In 1977, he was assistant trainer to Irish maestro Vincent O'Brien. That was the year The Minstrel won the Epsom Derby and Gosden, playing his part, led the colt to the start.
After a stint training in California, Gosden came back to England in 1988 and took out a licence.
The Epsom Derby kept on haunting him. In 1995, Tamure looked all over the winner until being swamped in the dying seconds of the race by Lammtarra.
"I am not an over-emotional person. When you think you have won the Derby and it gets snatched off you in the last 10 yards, you learn to be pretty hard inside," Gosden confessed.
But he finally tasted the fruits of victory when Benny The Dip, enterprisingly ridden by Willie Ryan, set sail for home up the Epsom straight and just held on to lift the $970,000 spoils.
This time the fates were really smiling on Gosden who nearly never got to train the colt because owner-breeder Landon Knight once wanted to sell Benny The Dip at the sales.
But the Ohio newspaper magnate, confined to a wheelchair since he contracted polio as a child, asked Gosden to take a look before the final decision.

Gosden missed the plane home and although aware Benny The Dip would make a lot of money at the sales, the trainer made it clear he adored the horse. "Landon asked me if I really loved the horse and he said that I could have him," Gosden recalled with evident relief.
The icing was added to the cake after Benny The Dip's last-gasp victory on Saturday.
Ebullient Italian jockey Frankie Dettori, who has shared so many triumphs with Gosden, rushed over, reached up to the towering trainer and gave him a huge bear hug of pure delight.
Lady Luck had smiled at last in one of the cruellest and most haphazard of sports. The name Gosden was finally written into the record books of the Epsom Derby.
